purpose: Frozen blind set measured once per system, never used for tuning. Scope: source-heldout (FT answer passages excluded), not unseen-evidence (FT context overlap allowed). Curated from the frozen corpus without running any retriever or model.

cases.query: What does Buffett say book value measures, and what does intrinsic business value measure instead?

gold_claims.claim: Book value records the accumulated financial input from contributed capital and retained earnings.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1983 letter; unit=qualitative accounting concept; definition=book value as accumulated financial input, not an estimate of future payoff.

gold_claims.claim: Intrinsic business value is an economic concept estimating future cash output discounted to present value.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1983 letter; unit=qualitative valuation concept; definition=discounted future cash output, i.e. what can be taken out of the business.

cases.verification_note: 1983_p0024 defines book value as input and intrinsic business value as discounted cash output, illustrated by two equally funded college educations.

cases.query: Why can an insurer that is already insolvent keep operating for years without running out of cash, in Buffett's 1984 account?

gold_claims.claim: Insolvent insurers do not run out of cash until long after they have run out of net worth, so they can be broke but flush.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1984 letter; unit=qualitative insurance-solvency mechanism; definition=cash arrives at policy inception while losses are paid much later, so cash outlasts net worth.

cases.verification_note: 1984_p0085 explains that premiums arrive up front and claims are paid later, letting insolvent insurers stay liquid after net worth is gone.

cases.query: Why does Buffett give little credit to a CEO who quadrupled earnings when the business only earns ordinary returns on capital?

gold_claims.claim: A CEO who quadrupled earnings may simply reflect years of retained earnings and compound interest rather than managerial achievement.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1985 letter; unit=qualitative managerial-performance critique; definition=earnings growth from retained capital at ordinary returns, not superior performance.

cases.verification_note: 1985_p0057 argues that growth from retained earnings at ordinary returns is no great managerial achievement, comparing it to quadrupling a savings account.

cases.query: What conditions define an economic franchise in Buffett's view, and how does a company reveal that it has one?

gold_claims.claim: An economic franchise sells a product or service that is needed or desired, has no close substitute and is not subject to price regulation.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1991 letter; unit=qualitative franchise conditions; definition=three simultaneous conditions: needed, no close substitute, not price regulated.

gold_claims.claim: A franchise is demonstrated by the ability to price aggressively and earn high rates of return on capital.
required_terms: high rates of return on capital
gold_claims.verification_note: 1991 letter; unit=qualitative test of a franchise; definition=pricing power shown in earning high returns on capital.

cases.verification_note: 1991_p0023 lists the three franchise conditions and the pricing-power test that reveals them.

cases.query: How did Buffett explain what went wrong with Berkshire's USAir holding in his 1992 letter?

gold_claims.claim: Industry economics had soured before the ink dried on our USAir check, and airline leaders engaged in prolonged kamikaze behavior.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1992 letter; unit=qualitative investment post-mortem; definition=blame placed on soured industry economics and competitor behavior, with Buffett accepting that no one pushed him.

cases.verification_note: 1992_p0082 states that airline economics soured right after the commitment and that Buffett jumped in voluntarily.

cases.query: Why did Buffett think so many CEOs fudged earnings in the late 1990s, and what insurance-industry maneuver did he use as an illustration?

gold_claims.claim: A growing number of managers think it is okay to manipulate earnings to satisfy Wall Street, and even their duty.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1998 letter; unit=qualitative accounting-ethics observation; definition=earnings manipulation framed as satisfying Wall Street rather than a Berkshire practice.

gold_claims.claim: A buyer of a property-casualty company may increase its loss reserves at acquisition, setting up later earnings as reserves are released.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1998 letter; unit=qualitative accounting illustration; definition=reserve boost at acquisition that later flows back into income.

cases.verification_note: 1998_p0076 describes managers manipulating earnings for Wall Street while 1998_p0084 gives the acquisition-reserve example.

gold_claims.verification_note: 2005 letter; unit=qualitative fable; definition=a fourth class of paid advisers claiming the earlier Helpers lack motivation.

cases.verification_note: 2005_p0115 gives the hyper-Helpers' explanation that brokers, managers and consultants are insufficiently motivated.

cases.query: What did Buffett say happened to America's investment income account in 2006, and what political reaction did he fear it might trigger?

gold_claims.claim: The U.S. investment income account, positive in every previous year since 1915, turned negative in 2006 because Foreigners now earn more on their U.S. investments than we do abroad.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2006 letter; unit=qualitative balance-of-payments indicator; definition=net income on investments held across borders, turning negative for the first time in the cited run.

gold_claims.claim: Buffett believed workers and voters would eventually find the annual tribute so onerous that a severe political backlash would follow, and expecting a soft landing is wishful thinking.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2006 letter; unit=qualitative political risk; definition=backlash from servicing the debtor position, not a prediction of market timing.

cases.verification_note: 2006_p0103 reports the investment-income account turning negative and 2006_p0104 predicts a political backlash and no soft landing.

cases.query: Why did Buffett expect stocks to outperform long-term bonds, and what caveat did he attach to that view?

gold_claims.claim: If current rates and low corporate tax rates persist, equities will almost certainly perform far better than long-term, fixed-rate debt.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2019 letter; unit=qualitative asset-class expectation; definition=stocks versus long-term fixed-rate bonds over coming decades given current rates and taxes.

gold_claims.claim: The caveat is that anything can happen to stock prices tomorrow, including major drops of perhaps 50% magnitude.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2019 letter; unit=qualitative risk warning; definition=short-term price drops of 50% magnitude that investors must tolerate.

cases.verification_note: 2019_p0055 gives the equities-over-bonds expectation and 2019_p0056 attaches the warning about 50% market drops.
